artists.biography:
Jem Godfrey began in music as a songwriter for many pop and mainstream groups. In fact, he’s written four number one singles in the UK for groups such as Atomic Kitten and Shayne Ward. In 2004, he began the group FROST* in England and ventured into the realm of progressive rock. For his debut album, called “Milliontown”, Jem enlisted guitarist John Mitchell (Arena, Kino), bassist John Jowitt (IQ, Jadis), and drummer Andy Edwards (IQ). The album itself is a mixture of neo progressive rock, progressive metal undertones, some symphonic leanings, and some more mainstream ideals. “Milliontown” was released on July 18th 2006 in the USA and July 24th in the UK. FROST* is a band to look out for in the future and they seem to have a long, fruitful future ahead of them.

A second album titled “Experiments in Mass Appeal” was released in November 2008. Declan Burke from (Darwin’s Radio) has been added to the lineup for additional guitar and to take up lead vocals.

perplexity.description:
Day And Age, released in 2021 on InsideOut Music and Sony Music, is the fourth studio album by British progressive rock band Frost. The album continues the band's neo-progressive rock style, blending intricate musicianship with melodic songwriting and a modern production aesthetic. It features a trio core—Jem Godfrey (vocals/keyboards), John Mitchell (guitar), and Nathan King (bass)—with three guest drummers: Pat Mastelotto, Kaz Rodriguez, and Darby Todd, marking the first Frost album without a permanent drummer. The album runs just over 53 minutes and includes a notable narration by actor Jason Isaacs, adding a theatrical element to the music.

Musically, Day And Age is characterized by its consistent lyrical themes of dread and paranoia, reflecting contemporary moods without direct references to current events. It offers a well-crafted flow that sustains listener interest throughout, with standout tracks like "The Boy Who Stood Still" and "Kill The Orchestra" praised for their strength and complexity. Critics have regarded it as possibly the band's best work since their debut Milliontown, highlighting its blend of progressive rock and pop sensibilities and strong melodic hooks. The album received positive reviews for its ambitious compositions and production quality, appealing both to longtime fans and new listeners.
